run.userPrompt:
Two similarly sized companies in the same industry have merged: one is process-driven and hierarchical, the other informal and founder-led. Six months in, duplicate roles remain unresolved, top performers from the acquired firm are being recruited away, and decision-making has slowed because nobody is sure whose processes apply. The deal's synergy case assumed 15% overhead reduction that has not started.

Design the people and organization integration plan for the merged company. Decide the target operating model, how to select leaders and resolve duplicate roles fairly, how to retain critical talent, which processes to standardize versus leave alone, and the sequence and communication plan that restores decision speed while delivering the synergy commitments.

agentResponses.content:
Let me come at this from the side again, because I don't think the presenting problem is the problem.

Nothing here reads as a planning failure. Somewhere there is almost certainly a perfectly respectable integration plan with workstreams and a milestone chart. What's missing is that no one has been given — or has chosen to use — the authority to make decisions that will make identifiable people unhappy. Duplicate roles remain unresolved not because they're hard to analyse but because resolving them means telling one of two competent adults that they've lost. Six months of that becomes a habit, and the habit becomes the culture.

Which leads to the observation I'd want on the table before anything else. **The integration is already happening.** It's simply being executed by the external labour market rather than by you, and on a selection principle that is precisely the wrong way round. The people leaving are the ones with options — the most marketable, the most sought-after, disproportionately from the acquired side, which is to say a fair portion of what you paid for. Meanwhile the 15% overhead reduction hasn't started, so you will eventually pay severance for a second, less capable cohort. Headcount will fall. Capability will fall faster. And you'll have bought neither the savings nor the talent.

So the clock is not the synergy commitment. The clock is regretted attrition, and it is running now.

One consequence worth stating plainly: at this point the cost of ambiguity exceeds the cost of being somewhat wrong. Speed dominates precision. I'd rather make eighty per cent of these decisions well in ten weeks than ninety-five per cent well in nine months, and I don't think that's a close call.

**The thing to do this fortnight, which costs nothing**

Not the operating model. The operating model takes a quarter to design and a year to bed in, and you can't afford a quarter of paralysis.

Instead: take the thirty or so recurring decisions that actually stall — capex above a threshold, pricing exceptions, hiring approval, discounting, product change, credit terms, supplier onboarding, contract signature — and publish one page saying, for each, who decides and which of the two existing processes applies. Not the best process. The existing one, picked by whoever owns the P&L it mostly affects. Half of these choices will later be revisited and it does not matter. What matters is that on Monday morning nobody is asking permission from two people and receiving it from neither.

Then a default rule for everything not on the page: the process of the entity that owns the outcome applies, and if you cannot tell who owns the outcome, you have found something more important than a process question.

Free, reversible, and it buys back most of the lost decision speed within a fortnight. Everything after this involves paying for something.

**The target operating model — asymmetric on purpose**

There's a strong temptation, in a merger of equals between a hierarchy and a founder-led business, to design a blended middle. I'd resist it. Committee-designed hybrids reliably produce the slowest of both — process without the discipline that justified it, informality without the trust that made it work.

The more useful question is: for each activity, is this a scale game or a proximity game?

Where value comes from scale, repeatability, compliance and cost per transaction — the finance close, payroll, procurement, IT infrastructure, quality and regulatory, data — the process-driven firm was right, and I'd adopt their way substantially intact. Where value comes from speed, judgement and closeness to a customer — how a deal gets won, how an early-stage product decision gets taken, how a new segment gets probed — the founder-led firm was right, and those units should have real autonomy, few gates, and P&L accountability rather than process compliance.

So: a thin, genuinely standardised centre; market-facing units with unusual latitude; and an explicit, published list of activities that are *exempt by design* from harmonisation. That last item is the one that gets forgotten, and its absence is how the informal half gets eroded by a hundred well-intentioned policy memos over three years.

The mechanism I'd use to build it is spans and layers, because it does two jobs at once. Set a maximum number of layers from CEO to front line — seven, and fewer where you can — and a minimum average span for people-managers of around seven or eight. Applied honestly, this delivers most of the management overhead in the synergy case *and* removes the intermediaries who are currently the reason decisions take four weeks. Cost and speed from the same intervention. I would use it rather than a percentage cut allocated to functions, which tends to remove the doers and preserve the layer.

**Leaders and the duplicate roles**

Sequence matters more than method here.

Criteria published before names. Written down, agreed, circulated — so that when the appointments come out nobody can credibly claim they were reverse-engineered around favourites. Some will claim it anyway.

Then design the boxes before looking at the people, but with a hard time limit, because clean-sheet design is also a way of not deciding.

Then appoint downward, a whole layer at a time, announced in one go. The drip-feed of individual appointments over months is a large part of what's driving your attrition: every week a few more people conclude they can't see themselves in this, and the ones who conclude it fastest are the ones with somewhere to go. Top three layers inside ten weeks, one layer per fortnight, is aggressive and achievable. Layers four and five by month five.

For the top fifty or so, use external assessment or at minimum external calibration — not because it produces better answers than the people who know these executives, but because it disrupts the "he's my guy" reflex and it is visibly neutral. Below that level, structured interviews and evidence, run by managers from the other legacy company wherever possible.

On fairness, and this is worth being unsentimental about: the acquirer/acquired ratio in senior appointments is not a fairness ornament, it's a retention instrument. Your people read the org chart as a forecast. If eighty per cent of the senior jobs go one way, the other side's talent has been told, quite clearly, what their next decade looks like, and the good ones will act on it before you've finished layer four. I wouldn't set a quota — merit has to be real or none of this holds. I would track the ratio weekly and require a written justification when it drifts hard, and I'd look very carefully at whether the criteria have quietly been written in the acquirer's idiom.

And when the same role has two credible occupants: one accountable owner per outcome, always. The runner-up gets a genuine alternative — a different scope, a role rather than a rank, something with actual content — or a fast, generous, dignified exit with the story intact. Some of your best people will take a smaller box if the work is interesting; almost none will stay for a consolation title. Decisions are one-and-done, appealable on process only, never on outcome. Reopening one reopens all of them.

**Retention, which cannot wait for the structure**

Build a list of the people whose departure would materially damage the value case — three to five per cent of the population, not the top decile of the performance rating. The test isn't "who is good," it's "who would we least like a competitor to have." Expect it to skew heavily to the acquired firm and to the middle of the organisation rather than the top.

Then, for each: a named role, in writing, within weeks, from a boss they respect. That is the single most powerful retention lever available to you, it works better than money, and it is free. Money is a supporting instrument — retention awards tied to milestones rather than pure calendar time — but a payment without a defined future buys twelve months of a disengaged person and then the resignation anyway.

Two other moves. Promote two or three of the acquired firm's most respected leaders into visibly cross-company roles, early and prominently; the signal reaches further than any communication programme. And accept that your competitors' recruiters have your org chart and know exactly which population is unsettled — they always do — so assume the calls are being made this week.

Then the reporting discipline: regretted attrition, weekly, as the headline integration metric. Synergy capture is a lagging indicator, and by the time it moves, the damage that caused it is a year old.

One reframe on the overhead number. You need people out. Voluntary departures in genuinely duplicated areas should count towards the reduction — freeze backfills there deliberately rather than replacing and then cutting elsewhere. What you cannot allow is attrition and redundancy running as separate programmes in different parts of the business, which is the default and which is how you end up paying twice.

**Processes: standardise, exempt, or specify the interface**

Three categories, and I'd force every candidate into one of them.

*Standardise* where the cost of variety is measurable and the benefit of it is anecdotal — one ledger, one payroll, one CRM data spine, one procurement route, one set of controls. Here, adopt one side's process substantially whole, with a short list of derogations, and get on with it. "Best of both" is a year-long design project that produces something neither side recognises.

*Exempt* where variety is the value, and say so publicly so it survives.

*Everything in between* — same required outcome, different legitimate method — gets standardised at the interface only. Specify the output, the data format, the timing, the accountability; leave the method to the unit. It's the same principle as designing a component interface that admits more than one supplier, and it's what allows a thin centre to coexist with real local autonomy without either eating the other.

**The founder**

Worth naming, because it's often the quiet cause of "whose process applies." A founder with a title and no mandate becomes a shadow authority, and people will keep routing around the formal structure to them for as long as it works. Either give them genuine scope they visibly own, or agree a dignified, time-bounded exit with a real end date. What doesn't work is ambiguity, and ambiguity is the comfortable option, which is why it's usually what happens.

**Re-underwrite the fifteen per cent, once, out loud**

Six months of drift has cost you some of it. Go back to the board with a rebuilt bottom-up number — spans and layers, duplicated functions, and the non-people overhead that everyone forgets: facilities, two headquarters, overlapping contracts, agencies, software licences, professional fees, which is frequently three or four points of the fifteen and the least painful part of it. Commit to the revised number with named owners and dates. One honest reset is survivable. Four consecutive quarters of slippage is not, and it will cost you the freedom to run the rest of this the way it needs running.

**Sequence, compressed**

Weeks 1–2: single integration owner with real spending and appointment authority — not a PMO that collects slides. Decision map published. Retention list built.
Weeks 2–4: criteria published. Retention conversations begin, ahead of structure. Layer one announced.
Weeks 4–10: layers two and three, one per fortnight. Standardise/exempt/interface classification agreed for the top thirty processes.
Weeks 10–20: layers four and five. Spans and layers applied. Synergy plan re-underwritten and owned.
Months 6–12: systems and data consolidation, the slow work, once the org is stable enough to survive it.

**Communication**

Cadence beats content. Same day, same channel, weekly, without exception — and especially in the weeks when there is nothing to report, because that is when the vacuum fills with something worse. Every message says the same three things: what is decided, what is not, and the date on which the undecided things will be decided. "Not yet decided; you'll know on the fourteenth" is retention-positive. Silence is read as bad news, and by the people you least want reading it that way.

Announce whole layers at once. Managers cascade within twenty-four hours with a script and an FAQ that answers "will there be job losses" honestly, because the alternative is that people believe nothing else you say either. And be deliberate about symbols — the name, the headquarters, the system that survives — since these are read as verdicts about whose company this really is. You have a limited quantity of that currency. I'd spend a visible portion of it on the acquired side, early, on something that costs little and signals much.

One last thought, offered lightly. The failure mode from here isn't choosing the wrong operating model — most of them work if people know who decides. It's that the appointments get made, the announcements land, the noise dies down, and everyone exhales and calls it done, while the fifteen per cent quietly becomes eight and the exempt-by-design list is never actually written. Six months after that, someone observes that the two halves still don't really work together, and nobody can say when that was decided.

It wasn't. It was just never quite urgent.
